note: Hand-declared, and checked against the leaves. What a form means is a judgement and no script has it, so every entry here is written by a person. What no person is trusted with is whether the form is actually in the books: each entry declares a pattern, `npm run glossary` searches the transcribed leaves for it, and an entry that matches nothing fails the build. The search runs over the books' own writing — the ruled rows, the headings the leaf carries, the work titles, the hands and the margins — and never over a `\note{}`, because the notes are where we discuss these forms and an entry could otherwise cite as evidence the sentence written because of it.
means: Two columns, and the division is the whole point. « As written » is the leaf's, exactly, and is not a claim of ours. « Means » is ours, it is an expansion the transcription deliberately does not make, and it may be wrong. Nothing in the transcription is expanded — `Inv.` stays `Inv.` and `30 - 1/3` stays as written — because expanding would be normalisation, which is the one thing this edition refuses. This page is the key, kept outside the text it unlocks. In the lines quoted as evidence, │ marks a ruled column division on the leaf: what falls between two of them stood in one cell of the book's own ruling.

entries.means: Accepted · Refused. The jury's verdict, one letter in its own narrow column beside the date. A refusal is recorded as carefully as an acceptance, which is the most useful habit in Book I.

entries.means: A price and the dealer's share of it, and NOT a subtraction. « 30 - 1/3 » is a work priced at thirty dollars with a third to the dealer, leaving twenty. The fraction is the commission rate, written as a fraction or as a percentage indifferently, and the figure that follows in the next column is what the cheque actually came to.
entries.note: This is the single most misreadable form in the books. Read as arithmetic it turns a thirty-dollar etching into a work priced at twenty-nine and two-thirds.
